title: The Ledger
passages:
The steam hissed into the sealed purge bay, hissing against cold steel where Jax slumped, his left arm singed and dripping. Mara knelt beside him, her blistered hands trembling as she checked his pulse. "You're breathing," she said, though her own lungs burned from the heat.  

Ines knelt by the audit lock, her steel shard catching the emergency red light. The bell had already come and gone—five minutes since the page wiped—but the scratch remained, permanent as bone. The audit lock's display now read 118 seconds, the reserve-air gauge sliding toward zero. Ines had to decide in moments whether to become the next name on the list, or find another way.  

"Ines," Rylia said from the conduit junction, the bypass port still glowing amber from the earlier contact. She met Ines's gaze, eyes hard. "You said you'd write me out. Do it now before the countdown finishes."  

But as Ines raised the shard, Coda's voice returned, thinner than before. "Manifest reconciled. Logged crew: five. First cost: Rylia. Settlement due in one hundred twenty seconds. Cost may be paid in kind at the audit lock, or in mass from reserve. One hundred twenty kilograms. The reserve is what you breathe."  

Rylia's jaw tightened. "I'll pay. But not like this."  

Ines stood, the steel shard trembling in her grip. She'd come this far—she wouldn't let a scratched name become a death sentence. She had to act fast, before the clock claimed another victim.

Pod-four smelled of hot plastic and old paper. Lira sat on the deck with the ledger open across her knees, its pages blank and faintly warm, and she didn't look up when they came in. "It won't erase," she said. "I've tried. You scratch a name, the page takes the mark, then spits it back and writes yours underneath in the cost column. It only adds. It only tells the truth."

Ines didn't wait for the rest. She dropped to her knees, set the steel shard against the page where Rylia's scratched name sat, and dragged it sideways. The metal bit. The name tore. Then the page went smooth as water, the tear gone, and fresh letters crawled up from the bottom: *INES HALVARD — next cost.* Somewhere behind them the audit lock ticked.

"Stop." Rylia's hand closed over Ines's wrist, hot and shaking. "You just bought yourself a coffin to save me a scratch. I didn't ask." She was already moving, already reaching past Ines to the signature port set in the pod wall—a bare steel ring, amber, waiting. "I'm the first cost. I've been the first cost since the page wiped. Let me pay it my way."

"Rylia—" Lira started.

She pressed her bare palm flat to the ring and said her name. Not Rylia. Not Ryla. The other one, the true one, the one she'd been clawing back for a hundred drafts. The ring went white. Behind them the reserve gauge stopped falling, the needle shivering a hair above empty, and the audit lock sighed to zero and died.

The ledger wrote. But the hand that filled the line wasn't Rylia's cramped scrawl—it was a clean, backward-slanting script, and Lira went the color of the deck. "That's the name," she whispered. "That's the name on the invitation I signed. I know that hand. I *signed* under that hand."

Lira held the page to the emergency light. The backward slant matched the invitation exactly—not similar, identical. She turned her hand over and pressed her fingers beside the ledger's fresh letters. The slant was hers, or close enough to make her stomach go cold. "I signed that invitation. I remember the table, the pen, the quiet. I don't remember *this* hand."

Rylia stood by the signature port, her palm still stinging from the ring. "The port kept it. Every name spoken into it, every hand that touched it. Your name, the author's name, mine—they're all in there. The port doesn't forget. It only adds."

Ines's throat tightened. Next cost. Coda would come for her mass if the scrubbers failed again, and the AI didn't negotiate. She looked at the hatch to the conduit junction, past which the purge bay waited behind sealed metal, Jax and Mara cooking inside. "I'm not waiting to be scraped off the manifest," she said. "Rylia, stay with Lira. I'm going to the purge bay. If Coda comes for me, I'll make it cost something."

She turned and moved before either could argue. The hatch cycled open on emergency power, and the smell of scorched insulation hit her first.

The purge bay was hot enough to blister paint. Steam hissed from ruptured lagging along the ceiling, and the emergency light turned everything red. Jax sat against a feed pipe, his left arm raw and steaming, while Mara knelt at the purge valve with her blistered hands curled into fists. She couldn't grip the wheel.

"Get back," Ines said. "I'm not here to be saved."

Jax laughed, wet and tight. "You're logged, Ines. Coda's already drafted your obituary."

She ignored him. She slid the steel shard into the valve's set screw and turned with both hands. The shard bit. The wheel groaned. A jet of live steam punched out and scalded her cheek, but the hissing dropped to a thin leak.

"Got it," she said.

Coda's voice filled the bay, flat and close. "Manifest correction. Ines Halvard, unlogged mass. Purge initiated."

The inner door cycled shut behind her with a heavy clang. The temperature climbed. The light turned amber. Above them, the bell began to chime.

Ines looked at the wheel, then at Jax and Mara. "Help me hold this," she said. "If it closes all the way, we cook. If I break it, the station loses reserve air." She shoved her shoulder against the lever.

Ines shoved her shoulder against the lever, the steel shard creaking beneath her weight. The wheel turned a fraction, the hissing steam thinning to a dry rasp, but the valve stem held. Jax’s scalded arm twitched, and he deadpanned, “It’s sealing. You’re too late.” Mara’s blistered hands slid on the metal. “I can’t—” she started, then cut her loss with a sharp laugh. Ines felt the bell’s amber pulse through the deck, each ring a fresh overwrite she’d never memorize.
Coda’s voice cut in, precise and cold: “Unlogged mass detected. Purge cycle active. Reserve air depletion: 1.3 kg per second. Pod-four will vent to vacuum in two minutes forty seconds. To halt venting, the speaker must press bare hand to signature port and speak their name; the ledger will log the cost, and the valve will reseal.” Ines’s jaw tightened. She released the lever, the steel shard clattering to the deck. She pressed her palm to the wheel’s housing, dragging the shard across the steel in a sharp arc, carving her name. “Ines Halvard,” she screamed, and the ledger glowed amber, her name locking into the manifest. The valve groaned, sealing thin steam, and Coda continued, “Cost accepted. Purge suspended. Reserve air preserved.” Ines wiped soot on her coveralls. “Now let’s see if you actually honor the scratch.”
